newsitem.title: UK: Timing of Iraqi crude exports is key for prices.
newsitem.headline: Timing of Iraqi crude exports is key for prices.

text.p: A quick resumption of Iraqi crude oil exports under a U.N. limited sales deal will not put pressure on tight winter markets, but prices could be hit if it is delayed, oil analysts and industry sources said on Tuesday.

Iraq said on Monday it was poised to export crude from its mothballed oil fields some time in December for the first time since a U.N. ban six years ago. This was after it agreed to U.N. conditions for the "oil-for-food" plan.
"It all depends on the timing. If we think the (Iraqi) oil is going to come out in the first quarter of 1997, then it is already factored in and it won't be a big deal," an oil industry source said.
A delay into the second quarter, when demand begins to taper off, would push prices lower and effectively end the recent bull run that has taken oil prices to five-year highs, he added.

Oil industry sources say Iraq's forecast appeared too optimistic and they doubted Iraqi oil would be seen any time before January, considering U.N. inspectors have yet to submit reports on the state of Iraq's oil facilities.

Issam al-Chalabi, Iraqi oil minister when Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, said under the pricing formula submitted to the U.N. and at current prices, Iraq would export around 500,000 barrels per day (bpd).

This is 2-300,000 bpd below the amount factored in by the market in September when the partial oil sales deal was shelved because of fears over security of U.N. personnel in northern Iraq during factional Kurdish fighting involving Iraqi troops.
The accord, finalised in May, would allow Iraq to sell $2 billion in oil over six months to buy food and medicine.
Much of the Iraqi crude will be exported via a pipeline through Turkey, which Ankara said on Tuesday was ready to take the oil to the Ceyhan Mediterranean terminal.
Among the remaining tasks are an inspection of oil metering equipment on December 5 to ensure faulty equipment at the Sakho station along the Iraq-Turkey border is operational.

Chalabi, speaking from his consultancy in Amman, Jordan, said first deliveries will be to Turkish refineries, which have put in for 2.1 million tonnes of Iraqi crude for the first six months of the renewable U.N. plan.

The surplus would be exported mainly to European and Mediterranean markets, traditional buyers of Iraqi crude oil before Gulf War sanctions locked out Iraqi production of 3.14 million bpd under their then OPEC quota.

"Oil going to other markets from the Mina al-Bakr terminal in the Gulf won't be for some time....I would assume that some oil would go to the Far East but this will be some time after January," Chalabi added.
Ministers from the 11 producer members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) are meeting in Geneva on Wednedsay to agree an output ceiling for the first half of 1997.
The market expects the cartel, founded in Baghdad in 1960, to freeze output at 25.03 million bpd, a ceiling which takes into account 800,000 bpd of Iraqi exports.

But analysts say OPEC is producing above its ceiling. And while consumer countries low on stocks have absorbed up to 800,000 extra barrels minus Iraq so far, the supply/demand balance when non-OPEC supply starts to creep up is less bright.

The market's ability to asborb the OPEC leakage was shown in its reaction to the possibility of imminent Iraqi sales with prices on Tuesday holding steady at $22.50-$22.60 a barrel, virtually unchanged from Monday.

The pricing formula agreed with the U.N. would price Iraq's Kirkuk grade crude at $1.3-$1.5 a barrel below benchmark Brent Blend. Basra Light, the other export grade, would be against an average of Oman and Dubai crudes for Far Eastern clients.
Trade sources said Romania and Bulgaria were likely clients of Iraqi crude while Spanish, Portuguese, Italian and French refiners running comparable Russian oil were also likely buyers.
Iraq would compete with Russian Urals oil, which at current prices would lose market share to Iraq, and Iranian light crude.
